title: They stood between broken people… and a perfect Savior.
paragraphs: They stood between broken people… and a perfect Savior.

Not enemies.
Not Pharisees.
Disciples.
Men who walked with Jesus. Ate with Him. Heard His voice. Saw His miracles.
And still… they tried to control who could come close.

Mark 10:13 says, “And they were bringing children to Him that He might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them.” Imagine that moment. Dust rising in the air. Mothers carrying hope in their arms. Little hands reaching.
Then a wall.

Not Roman soldiers.
Not religious elites.
Followers of Jesus.
Blocking the way.
Why?
Maybe they thought they were protecting His time. Maybe they believed some people weren’t “important enough.” Maybe they assumed access to Jesus had to be managed, filtered, controlled.
But Scripture doesn’t soften what happened next.
Jesus was indignant.
That word is heavy. It means deeply moved with righteous anger. Not irritated. Not mildly disappointed.
He was stirred to His core.
And He said, “Let the little children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:14).
Don’t miss that.
The only people Jesus publicly rebuked in that moment… were the ones trying to limit access to Him.
Let that sit.
Because this wasn’t just about children.
This was about the heart of the Gospel.
We think the danger is people running from Jesus.
But sometimes… the greater danger is people being blocked from Him by those who claim to represent Him.
And if we’re honest—
We’ve done this.
Not with ropes or barriers.

But with looks.
With words.
With silence.
With pride.
We’ve made the addict feel like they need to get clean before they come.
We’ve made the broken feel like they need to fix themselves before they’re welcomed.
We’ve made the sinner feel like they need to perform before they belong.
But the Gospel never said, “Clean yourself, then come.”
It says, “Come, and be made clean.”
Jesus said in Matthew 11:28, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
All.

Not the polished.
Not the impressive.
Not the already-fixed.
All.
But here’s where it cuts deeper.
Sometimes the “rebuke” isn’t loud.
It’s subtle.

A cold shoulder at church.
A judgmental whisper.
A refusal to sit beside someone “too messy.”
A theology that sounds right… but feels like a locked door.
We preach grace… but practice distance.
We sing about the cross… but act like we’re still the gatekeepers.
And that is dangerous.
Because Acts 4:12 declares, “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.”
If Jesus is the only way—
Then blocking people from Him is not a small mistake.
It’s a spiritual tragedy.
But here’s what we often miss…
The same disciples who tried to block others…
Were later used by God to bring thousands to Christ.
Peter, who once misunderstood access, stood up in Acts 2 and preached—and about 3,000 souls were saved.
Grace didn’t just correct them.
Grace transformed them.
And that means there is hope for us.

If you’ve ever judged instead of welcomed…
If you’ve ever filtered instead of invited…
If you’ve ever acted like access to Jesus depended on your approval…
You’re not beyond redemption.
But you are being called to repentance.
Because the cross settled this already.
When Jesus died, the veil in the temple was torn from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51). Not partially.
Fully.
Access was no longer restricted.

Not by status.
Not by background.
Not by past.
Through Christ, the way to God was opened for anyone who would repent and believe.
Ephesians 2:13 says, “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.”
Brought near.

Not pushed away.
Not screened.
Not evaluated by human standards.
Near.
So the question is no longer theological.
It’s personal.
Are you making it easier… or harder… for people to meet Jesus?
Are you pointing people to Him—
Or positioning yourself in front of Him?
Because Jesus is still saying today:
“Let them come.”
The addicted.
The doubting.
The ashamed.
The curious.
The ones who don’t look like they belong.
Let them come.
And don’t you dare stand in the way of a soul He died to save.
This is not about lowering standards.
It’s about lifting up the Savior.
Because when people truly encounter Jesus—
He does the transforming.
Not us.
John 6:37 says, “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.”
Never.

Not once.
Not ever.
So we don’t get to cast out who Jesus invites in.
We don’t get to filter who grace has already made a way for.
We don’t control access.
We carry the invitation.
So open the door.
Drop the pride.
Kill the silent judgments.
And start bringing people to Jesus like your life depends on it—
Because theirs might.
